lines.say: Your circuit is ready, and you want to run it on a real chip.
Here's the catch. On a chip, not every qubit can reach every other.
Picture a long dinner table, where guests can only chat with their neighbours.
To reach the far end, they trade seats, risking a spilled drink every time.
A chip is the same. Wires join only neighbouring qubits, a wiring diagram called the coupling map.
A gate on two qubits, like C NOT, only works along a wire.
What if your circuit needs a C NOT between qubits that aren't neighbours?
Qiskit's transpiler, which fits your circuit to the chip, adds swap gates.
A swap trades the states of two neighbours, like guests trading seats. Moving states like this is called routing.
Take four qubits in a row, and a C NOT from first to last.
Two swaps walk the first state along until it's beside the last. Then the C NOT runs.
But each swap costs three C NOTs, so one gate has become seven.
Every C NOT adds a little noise, a small chance of error, so more gates mean a noisier answer.
Here the dinner table breaks down, because a guest could always just shout.
A chip has no shortcut. Far apart qubits can't interact until their states sit side by side.
The rewritten circuit may look different, but it computes the same thing. Only the noise has grown.
So keep qubits that work together close, and keep circuits short.
Chips connect only neighbours, routing adds swaps, and every swap adds noise.
